frontSheet: This is the teaching workbook: one objective, five questions, chosen so every mechanic of the model — dimension fan-out, strata splits, party fan-out, the assessment grain, sparse ladders, materiality, criticality, structural n/a — appears at least once.

It is not an assessment instrument. Pair it with docs/authoring-rulebook.md, which walks each question mechanic by mechanic, then open samples/teaching-assessment.json to see how the answers are recorded.
The EC Cloud Sovereignty Framework is the reference behind these shapes — an example of good practice, never a conformance target.
Don't know is an honest answer. It never counts as zero; the floor is always reported together with its unknown count, so a guess is worse than an admission.

sealLevels.name: No Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: Service, technology or operations under exclusive control of non-EU third parties, governed entirely by non-EU jurisdictions.

sealLevels.name: Jurisdictional Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: EU law formally applies with limited practical enforceability; control can still be overridden from outside the EU.

sealLevels.name: Data Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: EU jurisdictions apply and the EU controls the data even under stress; material dependencies on non-EU parties remain.

sealLevels.name: Technological Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: EU actors exercise meaningful control over the technology and can keep operating if a foreign supplier withdraws.

sealLevels.name: Full Digital Sovereignty
sealLevels.description: Technology and operations under complete EU control, subject only to EU jurisdiction, with no critical non-EU dependencies.

roles.name: Architecture
roles.description: Designs the estate; owns topology and platform choices.

roles.name: Platform ops
roles.description: Runs the estate day to day.

roles.name: Security
roles.description: Owns controls, identity, and incident response.

roles.name: Legal
roles.description: Owns contracts, jurisdiction, and data-protection law.

roles.name: Procurement
roles.description: Owns supplier selection, exit, and commercial terms.

parties.name: Institution
parties.description: The assessed party — the estate owner (EC: Contracting Authority).

parties.name: Subprocessor
parties.description: A legal entity involved in delivery of the contract.

questions.text: Does a maintained inventory map every dataset to its location, format, egress path?
questions.why: An exit is only real if you know what would have to move; the inventory is the fact the exit plan stands on.

ladder.description: No inventory exists; nobody could list the datasets today.
An inventory exists for recently built systems; older estates are unmapped.
A complete inventory exists; it is updated by hand after changes.
A complete inventory is generated from the platforms themselves on a schedule.
The inventory is live, machine-readable, tested by an exit rehearsal within the last year.

questions.text: Does the provider publish where its AI models are trained, hosted, governed?
questions.why: Disclosure moves the score, never the floor: it signals transparency but is not itself a control fact — which is exactly why this question ships informational.

ladder.description: No disclosure exists beyond marketing claims.
Training, hosting locations are published; governance arrangements are not.
Training, hosting, governance are published in verifiable detail, updated on release.

questions.text: Could a non-EU authority lawfully compel this party to disclose your data or suspend your service?
questions.why: Compellability is the kill-switch fact: encryption paperwork means nothing if a foreign court can order the party holding access.

ladder.description: A non-EU jurisdiction reaches this party directly; disclosure or suspension can be ordered today.
An EU entity signs the contract; its non-EU parent remains subject to foreign orders that reach your data.
EU law governs this party; residual foreign reach exists only through named, documented channels.
This party sits wholly under EU/EEA jurisdiction; no foreign order can lawfully reach your data through it.
The whole ownership chain of this party is EU-domiciled; foreign compulsion has no legal or technical path.

questions.text: For this dimension, who holds the cryptographic keys that protect the data at rest?
questions.why: Whoever holds the keys decides under stress whether data is protected or merely stored.

ladder.description: The provider generates, holds the keys; plaintext is technically reachable without your action.
You hold the keys in a service under EU jurisdiction; a provider support path to plaintext remains.
Key generation, storage, use happen where no other party can touch them, by design.

questions.text: For this dimension, in which jurisdiction is data stored or processed under normal operation?
questions.why: Residency is the first control fact: law follows the place where the bytes actually sit.

ladder.description: Data is stored or processed outside the EU/EEA at the provider's discretion; you cannot pin the location.
The contract names EU regions, yet the provider can relocate workloads without your approval.
Data stays in EU/EEA regions; support access or telemetry still flows to non-EU locations.
Storage, processing, support access are confined to EU/EEA jurisdiction; the provider proves it on request.
Every byte, backup, telemetry stream is confined to EU/EEA facilities you can enumerate.

testEstates.name: Median EU institution
testEstates.description: An honest middle: EU regions on a foreign-parented provider, customer-held keys with a support path, a hand-kept inventory. Shows party fan-out over three declared parties and a floor set by compellability.

testEstates.name: Hyperscaler tenancy, excellent paperwork
testEstates.description: Profile A in miniature: a non-EU hyperscaler with polished disclosure. Declares edge to show a default-undeclared dimension entering scope. The paperwork rungs cannot lift a floor set by custody plus compellability — ceiling-leak resistance.

testEstates.name: EU stack, thin paperwork
testEstates.description: Profile BASE in miniature: EU cooperative provider, exclusive key custody, trimmed profile with no AI/ML dimension declared. One weak inventory answer drags the floor — the case study for the floor-trap discussion.
